title: Agile
body:
The process model that assumes you got the requirements wrong. Instead of running the
[[SDLC]] once like [[Waterfall]] does, Agile runs all of it (analyse, design, build, test)
inside a short iteration, typically one to four weeks, and produces working software at the
end of every one. The user sees it, reacts, and that reaction becomes the input to the next
iteration.

The point is not speed. The point is shortening the gap between making a wrong decision and
finding out, because that gap is what makes defects expensive. Waterfall's gap is the whole
project; Agile's is one iteration.

## What follows from iterating

- **Requirements are a queue, not a document.** Work is kept as a prioritised backlog and
  re-ordered every cycle, so "the requirements changed" stops being a crisis.
- **[[YAGNI Principle]].** If you cannot predict next month's requirements, building for
  imagined futures is wasted work, so build only what this iteration needs.
- **Continuous testing.** [[Unit testing]] has to be automated, because the code is
  re-tested every iteration rather than once at the end.
- **Working software over documentation.** Not "no documentation": documentation that
  describes code that changes weekly goes stale faster than it gets read.
- **The customer is part of the team.** Feedback every cycle only works if someone is there
  to give it.

## Where it goes wrong

Iterating is not a substitute for having a direction. Without a prioritised backlog and
someone empowered to say no, Agile becomes "no plan", scope drifts every cycle, and the
architecture ends up as whatever the last twelve iterations happened to bolt on. The
discipline it removes from the schedule has to reappear as discipline about scope.

The vault has no notes on Scrum, Kanban, or extended practices like pair programming and
continuous integration; those are specific frameworks built on top of this idea, and this
course covered the idea.
